subtitle: Signs of compromise and what to do first.

subsections.title: If an Account Is Hacked
subsections.summary: Signs of compromise and what to do first.

blocks.html: Signs: settings or posts you didn’t change, contacts getting messages you didn’t send, your correct password being rejected, password-reset emails you didn’t ask for, or logins from places you’ve never been.

items.title: Stop using it for anything sensitive
items.text: Until you know what happened, assume someone else can read the account.

items.title: Change the password
items.text: Use a new, unique password from your password manager, and change it anywhere else you used the same one.

items.title: Sign out every other session
items.text: Find the account’s list of active sessions or devices and log out of everything you don’t recognise.

items.title: Check forwarding and recovery settings
items.text: Look for email forwarding rules, recovery emails or phone numbers you didn’t add — attackers use them to keep access.

items.title: Turn on two-factor authentication
items.text: Use an authenticator app or security key. See Auth / 2FA.

items.title: Unlink connected apps
items.text: Remove “Sign in with Google/Facebook/Apple” connections you don’t use, starting with financial and sensitive accounts.

items.title: Check your devices
items.text: Any phone or computer that was signed in could be the source. Update it and check for apps you don’t recognise.

items.title: Can’t get back in?
items.text: Use the service’s recovery process, then the Digital First Aid Kit. At-risk people can get free help from Access Now’s Digital Security Helpline.
